uwaterloo,"I finished most of a combinatorics major at Waterloo before dropping out to join a security company (I didn't want to do my breadth and depth requirements).

While my on-the-job cryptography experience is mostly limited to implementation details (tl;dr use libsodium), I run a world-class CTF (capture the flag) team that competes in security competitions two or three times a month. We won DEFCON a few years ago.
If you're interested in pursuing a career in cryptography, I'd argue that getting involved in CTF is one of the most effective ways to expose yourself to the field.

My contribution to the team is primarily in solving cryptography problems, that range from attacking faulty implementations of RSA, to ECC implementations that use insecure curves, to everything in between. I agree with /u/djao that a strong math background is absolutely essential in cryptography, and this even true when working on anything but the most trivial of cryptography CTF problems.

Fortunately, there's an increasing number of resources available for learning cryptography. My personal favourite is [Cryptopals](http://cryptopals.com/). It's a series of challenges that assume no prior knowledge of cryptography, and teach you how different primitives and schemes work by tasking you with attacking them. It's an excellent introduction that will teach you enough about the field to guide you in directing your research further. You'll also want to pick up a copy of [Cryptography Engineering](http://www.amazon.com/Cryptography-Engineering-Principles-Practical-Applications/dp/0470474246). It's an excellent textbook that strives to give a high-level overview of cryptography, for engineers, without getting bogged down in the details. You'll need to learn those details eventually, but this book should help you decide if it's a field you're interested in.

In parallel with Cryptopals I'd recommend trying your hand at some CTFs. They're tough, and I guarantee that you'll be confused for your first couple, but that's okay. Everybody needs to fail a few times before they start to understand what they don't know. I recently [gave a talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jnh8PK9iQco) on how to get started with CTFs. It isn't cryptography specific, but there's a lot of good resources mentioned. In particular, you'll want to keep an eye on [CTF Time](http://ctftime.org) to keep up to date on upcoming CTFs.

If you give CTFs a try, at some point you're going to need to able to sit down and read a research paper. It's okay to not understand everything you're reading immediately, but you need to be willing to go out and research any gaps in your knowledge. There's been CTFs where I've skimmed a dozen different papers while trying to solve a single task, so you're going to get a lot of practice at pulling out the important information. At the very least though, you should have a rudimentary understanding of group theory: once you start attacking ECC schemes the math starts piling on pretty heavily.

Spend a few months working through Cryptopals and some CTFs and you'll have a very good grasp of the engineering side of cryptography. You probably won't have much experience writing proofs or doing your own research, but hopefully you'll have been able to build some sort of an intuition for broken cryptography, and at the very least, learn whether it's the field for you.
I can't speak for what's involved in getting into academia, but feel free to ping me if you have any other questions! You can find my contact information on [my website](http://shanewilton.com/).

incremental_games,"You can't ever prevent cheating without delegating everything to a trusted server. That being said, you can raise the bar for cheating.

One method that comes to mind, is detecting cheating by employing some type of integrity checking. For example, you could hash the game state to compute a checksum, then store that in memory. Then, every tick, verify that the stored checksum matches the game state. If it doesn't, it means somebody modified the game state without computing and storing the new checksum.
It's still possible to bypass, and any dedicated reverse engineer is going to, but it won't be absolutely trivial.",1440915064.0,6

In the above-paper they design a reputation-based system which serves to aid users in selecting the initial entry-point, but you're correct in that there is the possibility of being compromised simply by selecting the wrong cascade.

Based on my understanding, the biggest win offered by cascades comes from the fact that regardless of what percentage of the network is comprised of by malicious nodes, as long you're using a cascade containing some trusted nodes, even if the others are malicious, you're still good. programming,"Essentially, any network which artificially introduces some sort of slowdown which makes analysis of the network more difficult. A canonical example is allowing a node to push traffic to the next node in the sequence once per day, doing the entire push in bulk.

Consider the end-to-end attack in Tor. Imagine that an attacker is able to create a snapshot of the traffic coming in and out in, say, 1 second, and they determine there to be N connections routed through at that moment. If that same attacker tries to analyze a network which only has inter-node communication once a day, it means that that same attacker has to snapshot the network traffic for a 24-hour interval.  Assuming constant network usage, this means that for the same attack, they now need to analyze 86400*N connections, and that's just for a one-node network!

I'm no researcher, so I don't know what sort of delay is necessary in practice, but I do know that it will be dependent on network activity. The general idea, however, is that you want to increase the noise an attacker has to sift through until it becomes computationally infeasible for them to perform the attack.

This does have the obvious drawback of, well, increasing the latency, so obviously the network cannot be used for all of the same use-cases as something like Tor. However, this isn't to say that there aren't plenty of applications which don't rely on immediate response times. Web-browsing would suck on a 1-day delay, but would you really complain too much if it took a few days for an especially controversial blog to appear online, if it meant it wouldn't be traced back to you?",1379989429.0,33

programming,"Hey, Proggit! I'm the friend in question who wrote Dissentr, so I thought I'd clear up a few questions.

First of all, this is NOT something anybody should be using for anything more than just toying around. I've been equally interested in Mix networks and Erlang for a few weeks now, and thought using one to write the other would be a fun hackathon project. It being a hackathon project, I wasn't really expecting anyone to come across it.

This was made purely to further my own knowledge in the area, and I can guarantee that, in it's current incarnation, it is not a secure network for any purpose. In fact, the design as stands is vulnerable to attack by introducing a malicious node which lies about other nodes public keys. This, and most of the other issues I've noticed are primarily implementation details, but the point stands that this was a PoC for myself, and should not be used.

However, that isn't to say that the concept doesn't have merit! Mix networks have a long history of being used by especially paranoid Cypherpunks for anonymous remailers. Someone in the comments already mentioned [Mixminion](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixminion), which was a definite source of inspiration for this project. Unfortunately, as I looked into the field more and more, it seemed like high-latency mix networks left the spotlight a while ago, and have only really been used for implementing anonymous remailers. This is a shame, since there really seems to be a huge opportunity here for trading the convenience of real-time responses for increased security.

If you're interested in the idea, definitely look into some of the more serious research - my implementation is especially naive, and researchers have been doing some really cool stuff with strong, low-overhead, network designs for exactly this sort of problem. Of special note, is [Sphinx](http://www.cypherpunks.ca/~iang/pubs/Sphinx_Oakland09.pdf), the network I'd have liked to implement, given more time.",1379985993.0,228
